newsitem.title: CANADA: Oil discovery fails to lift Arakis stock.
newsitem.headline: Oil discovery fails to lift Arakis stock.

text.p: Shares in Arakis Energy Corp were stuck their recent price range on Monday despite the company's announcement of a drilling success in Sudan.

Arakis, which is developing a US$1-billion oil project with a consortium formed in December, said its much-watched El Nar 2a well penetrated a gross oil column of 120 metres and had the potential to pump at a rate of 10,000 barrels per day.
The company's announcement, however, came as tensions between Sudan government forces and opposition rebels boiled over with intense fighting reported along the Ethiopian border.
Arakis shares on Nasdaq were up 1/32 in Monday trade to 3-29/32 on volume of 746,300 shares.

"I think the stock reacted to this well -- there were rumors a week or two weeks ago," said Bill Magee, analyst with Credifinance Securities in Toronto. "However, it has been depressed by the renewed rebel activity."
The fighting is concentrated several hundred miles north of Arakis's drilling operations at Heglig and Unity and several sources said company operations were not at immediate risk.
However, the military activity had added to investor jitters over the stock, sources said.
The fighting began eight days ago when the rebels, an alliance of northern and southern groups, launched an offensive aimed at paving the way for a popular uprising in the Sudan capital of Khartoum.

The El Nar well, the second of the consortium's 1997 drilling campaign, showed similar characteristics to Arakis's Toma South well, which flow tested at 10,000 barrels per day, th company said on Monday.
"It suggests they may have another 100 to 150 million barrel discovery," Magee said.

"Toma South is estimated at 130 million (barrels of reserves) and this appears similar, subject to delineation, which means a step-out (well) for confirmation. But that's the kind of order of magnitude that comes to mind."
Arakis in December announced it formed a joint venture with China National Petroleum Corp, Malaysia state oil company Petronas and the Sudan government.
Besides field development, the consortium's plans include building a 950-mile pipeline to the Red Sea from Southern Sudan.

Although Arakis said initial estimates placed the pipeline capacity at 150,000 barrels per day, chief executive John McLeod has suggested it may be far larger by the time a final decision is made in about six months.
